conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your 16th cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your brain lymphoma. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I'm okay, just a little tired. My foot pain has been worse this week, and I’ve had some blood in my stool again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We reviewed your recent colonoscopy—it showed mild inflammation in the rectum, but the rest of the colon looks normal. The polyps were removed, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I still bleeding? I restarted the mesalamine pills like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Because you’re getting methotrexate, we need to avoid anything that might slow its clearance. Oral mesalamine can interfere, so we’ve switched you to a rectal suppository form.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. Is that why I’m still bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The flare is mild, and the suppository should help target the area without affecting your chemo. We consulted GI, and they agree with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the methotrexate? I remember last time my liver enzymes went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve had mild transaminitis after past cycles. It’s expected and usually resolves. We’ll monitor your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot? It’s still burning, goes up my leg. MRI was normal, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your spine MRI, ultrasound, and spinal tap were all negative. It’s likely neuropathic pain. We’ll keep you on gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wish we knew what was causing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s frustrating when we can’t find a clear cause. But gabapentin helps many patients with similar symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my aspirin? I usually take it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your aspirin this admission. It can interfere with methotrexate clearance. You’ll restart it when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my mood’s been okay. I know last year was rough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. You’re still on citalopram, and Social Work checked in. You’re denying any depression or thoughts of self-harm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m stable. Just focused on getting through treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll give your chemotherapy around noon. You’ll get fluids to help protect your kidneys and liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel sick afterward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some patients get mild nausea. We’ll give anti-nausea meds beforehand and have more available if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just finished your methotrexate infusion. Everything went smoothly. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little flushed, but no nausea yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’re giving sodium acetate in your fluids to help alkalinize your urine and protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No IV bicarbonate? I thought that’s what they usually use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a national shortage, so we’re using sodium acetate instead. It works similarly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look good. Creatinine is stable at 0.7, so your kidneys are handling the chemo well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My foot’s still bothering me, but I guess that’s not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, and we don’t expect it to change quickly. We’ll keep your gabapentin going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver? Any updates?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. We’ll check your levels tomorrow. Mild elevations are expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the methotrexate level? When will that be safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We start checking 24 hours after the dose. Once it drops below 0.2, you can go home. Leucovorin rescue also helps clear it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helps 'rescue' the healthy cells, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It protects your bone marrow and gut from the chemo’s effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Great news—your methotrexate level is now 0.19. That means you’re safe to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s wonderful! What about my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ALT and AST are up a bit—43 and 44—but that’s mild and expected. They’ll likely return to normal in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood count? I’m always a little anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is 11.0, which is stable. It’s due to the chemo, but not low enough to need intervention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my potassium and phosphorus? I remember last time they were low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—they were slightly low, so we gave replacements. Now they’re normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So I can restart my aspirin when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, restart it tomorrow. But stop it two days before your next chemo admission to help the methotrexate clear better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the mesalamine? I’ll keep using the suppository?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use the rectal suppository at bedtime for the next two weeks. It targets the inflamed area without affecting your chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your asthma inhalers, gabapentin, citalopram, and the rest as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge orders are ready. You’re doing well—clear mental status, walking independently, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really glad. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Just remember: restart aspirin today, stop it two days before next chemo, and use the mesalamine suppository nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and GI if the bleeding continues. Otherwise, see you in a month for cycle 17.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Take care, and call if anything changes.
